[S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) fed the converter a constant voltage and
found that a board advertising 16 bits delivers about 11. That measurement
asked nothing of the converter's timing, because a constant does not care when
you look at it.

S2 puts a sinusoid in, fits it by least squares, and studies what is left
over. Every timing error is now an amplitude error, and it grows with
frequency — so the effective resolution falls as the signal gets faster, and
where it starts falling tells you whether the converter is limited by its
noise or by its clock. The same fit measures the board's oscillator against
the generator's, in parts per million.

The result the experiment exists for is a contrast: the **same samples**
analysed on the nominal sampling grid and on the device's own timestamps give
different effective resolutions, and the difference is what timestamping is
worth, in bits.

## What you measure {#sec-s2-index-measure}

| Quantity | How | Where it is used later |
|---|---|---|
| Dynamic ENOB against frequency | Four-parameter sine fit, residual RMS | The resolution to quote for any signal that moves |
| Timing penalty, in bits | The same fit on the nominal grid and on `t_us` | The argument for using timestamps, everywhere on this site |
| Aperture jitter $\sigma_j$ | Fit of the jitter limit to the high-frequency end | The ceiling no front-end improvement can lift |
| Noise/jitter crossover | Where the jitter limit meets S1's noise floor | [S3](../S3-aliasing-filtering/index.qmd)'s filter budget; M3's modal resolution |
| Clock accuracy [ppm] | $\hat{f}/f_\mathrm{gen} - 1$ | Every frequency this platform reports |

: What S2 produces {#tbl-s2-index-outputs}

## Bench {#sec-s2-index-bench}

**Tier 2.** S1's bench, plus a signal generator and the conditioning stage
that maps its bipolar output onto the converter's unipolar input — see
[the conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd).

**Board.** Streaming is required, and so is a high loop rate: the sweep has to
reach frequencies where jitter dominates, which means sampling in the tens of
kilohertz. That restricts this experiment to the mbed boards; see
[Supported boards](../../setup/boards.qmd).

**Host.** Linux recommended, for the reasons S1 measured.

::: {.callout-important}
## The generator must be better than the board

The residual of a fit cannot tell you whether an imperfection came from the
source or from the converter, so the source has to be the quieter of the two.
And never use the board's own DAC as the signal source: it shares the
reference, the clock and the ground with the ADC, so its errors are
correlated with the ones being measured, and the result looks excellent while
meaning nothing.
:::

## Reference data {#sec-s2-index-data}

Nine generated runs in `data/`, one per sweep point, each 2003 samples — a
prime, so that any number of signal cycles in the record is coprime with it
and the sampling is as close to coherent as a loop-driven sampler allows.

| File | Nominal frequency |
|---|---|
| `sweep-0010hz` … `sweep-0200hz` | 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 Hz — the noise-limited end |
| `sweep-0500hz`, `sweep-1000hz` | 500 Hz, 1 kHz — around the crossover |
| `sweep-2000hz`, `sweep-4000hz` | 2 kHz, 4 kHz — jitter limited |

: Reference data shipped with S2 {#tbl-s2-index-data}

The generator's exact frequency and amplitude, with their uncertainties, are
in each sidecar's `references[]` rather than in `channels[]`: the generator is
an instrument used to make the measurement, not a channel on the board.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The reference data is synthetic

It is produced by a seeded generator (`tools/synth/s2_daq_dynamic.py`) whose
parameters are plausible placeholders, not measurements — they are marked
`TODO (Paolo)` in `tools/synth/params/s2.yaml`. It exists so the analysis
templates render, and are checked in continuous integration, with no hardware
attached. Every page that uses it says so.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
## Instructor summary {.instructor-note}

Three hours, tier 2. Nearly all the difficulty is in the first twenty minutes
of generator setup — amplitude, headroom, and no clipping — so start the
groups on that immediately. The result worth the discussion time is the
timing penalty, not the ENOB itself. Full notes, expected values, common
failures and the rubric are in the
[handbook](handbook.qmd#sec-s2-instructor).
:::
